prompt.1: The agency that runs Metro Vancouver's buses and trains says it will run short of money soon. What should the province do?
prompt.2: TransLink, which runs Metro Vancouver's buses and trains, says it needs new money from 2028. What should the province do?
prompt.3: TransLink says it needs at least $112 million a year in new money from 2028. What should the province do about transit in Metro Vancouver?
prompt.4: TransLink's provincial top-up ends in 2027, and it says it needs at least $112 million a year more from 2028. What should the province do?
prompt.5: The province's $312 million subsidy carries TransLink to the end of 2027; the agency says it needs at least $112 million a year from 2028, and the government has ruled out a vehicle levy. Which approach?

context.1: TransLink runs the buses and trains in Metro Vancouver. The province gives it extra money now, but that runs out after next year. Parties disagree on who should pay after that, and on whether some riders should travel free.
context.2: TransLink, the regional transit agency, gets a provincial top-up that ends in 2027. From 2028 it needs at least $112 million a year more. In October the government ruled out a yearly fee on vehicles and a charge for using roads. Parties disagree on where the money should come from, and on free fares for young people and seniors.
context.3: The province's $312 million subsidy carries TransLink to the end of 2027. From 2028 the agency needs at least $112 million a year more. In October the NDP government ruled out a vehicle levy and road pricing and promised a law in 2027 to find another source, without naming one. The Conservatives oppose any new tax or levy. The Greens want free fares for riders under 25 and over 65. CentreBC promises more service and a pass credit.
context.4: The province gave TransLink $312 million in 2025, about half of its shortfall to the end of 2027. TransLink needs at least $112 million a year in new revenue from 2028 and says the province chooses the tool. Fuel use per vehicle has fallen about 45% since 2002, which erodes the fuel tax that funds transit. On October 2 the NDP ruled out a vehicle levy and road pricing and promised a 2027 revenue law. The Conservatives oppose any new tax. The Greens and CentreBC would spend more on service but name no new regional revenue source.
context.5: TransLink received $479 million from the province in March 2023 and $312 million for 2025 to 2027, and needs at least $112 million a year from 2028. A reported $100 to $150 yearly vehicle levy, collected at ICBC renewal, was never confirmed. On October 2, 2026 Eby said a vehicle levy or road pricing 'are not options we would proceed with' and promised legislation in 2027 for a 2028 revenue source, unnamed. The same week the NDP pledged a 10 cent a litre fuel tax cut, which the Greens say undercuts transit funding. The Conservatives' October 2 release opposed the levy and proposed no alternative. CentreBC's October 10 platform funds 15% more service inside a $15 billion three-year plan. OneBC has no transit position.

text.5: Keep the $312 million subsidy to 2027, legislate an as yet unnamed TransLink revenue source in 2027 for 2028, rule out a vehicle levy and road pricing, and cut the provincial motor fuel tax by 10 cents a litre.

prompt.1: A court says a First Nation has title, a kind of ownership right, to Richmond land with homes on it. What should happen?
prompt.2: A court recognized a First Nation's title to Richmond land with private homes. How should the province handle homeowners and title claims?
prompt.3: A 2025 ruling recognized Cowichan title over Richmond land with private homes. How should the province handle homeowners and title claims?
prompt.4: The Cowichan title ruling over Richmond land with homes is under appeal. How should the province handle homeowners and title?
prompt.5: In August 2025 the BC Supreme Court recognized Cowichan Tribes' Aboriginal title over Richmond land including privately held parcels; the province, Ottawa and Richmond have appealed. Which approach to homeowners and title?

context.1: A judge decided that a First Nation has title, a kind of ownership right, to some land in Richmond, including land under people's homes. The province is fighting that decision in a higher court. Parties disagree on what this means for the people who live there, and on how to settle these claims.
context.2: In 2025 the BC Supreme Court recognized Cowichan Tribes' title over land in Richmond, including private homes. The province, the federal government and the City of Richmond have appealed. Parties disagree on whether to promise homeowners money if their home loses value, whether to change the Indigenous rights law, and whether claims should be settled by treaty or in court.
context.3: The August 2025 Cowichan ruling recognized Aboriginal title over Richmond land that includes private homes. The province is appealing and Eby says it will 'go to the wall' for owners. CentreBC would pass a law promising owners compensation for lost value. The Conservatives and OneBC would repeal the Indigenous rights law and put property rights first. The Greens would keep the law and settle claims by negotiation. A March poll found most people would put private property first.
context.4: The Cowichan decision (BC Supreme Court, August 2025) recognized Aboriginal title over part of Richmond including privately held parcels; the province, Canada, Richmond and others have appealed. A separate 2025 Court of Appeal ruling made DRIPA obligations enforceable, and the two cases are often confused. Eby calls the rulings 'overreaching' and promises to protect owners, without a compensation law. CentreBC's homeowner guarantee would compensate owners up to assessed value and keep homes mortgageable. The Conservatives and OneBC would repeal DRIPA. The Greens would legislate how DRIPA is carried out. Angus Reid (March 2026): 65% put private property first.
context.5: Cowichan Tribes v. Canada (BC Supreme Court, August 2025) recognized Aboriginal title over land in Richmond including privately owned parcels; CentreBC's platform says about 145 private properties are affected. Cowichan Tribes, the province, Canada and Richmond have all appealed. The Court of Appeal's December 2025 Gitxaala decision made Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act duties enforceable; on April 20, 2026 Eby dropped plans to amend or suspend the Act for the spring session. On September 25 he said responding to the court 'is not up for debate'. Angus Reid, March 11 to 17, 2026 (n=499): 53% say the Act goes too far, 65% put private property rights first. OneBC's Property Rights Protection Act was defeated 40 to 48 on October 29, 2025, with Conservatives voting in favour.

prompt.1: Who should decide how many homes fit on a lot: the province or city councils?
prompt.2: The province makes cities allow several homes per lot and towers near transit. Keep that power, or give it back to councils?
prompt.3: Sixteen Metro Vancouver mayors want the 2023 density laws undone. Keep the rules, add to them, or give councils back the say?
prompt.4: Sixteen Metro Vancouver mayors asked in 2025 to repeal or revise the multi-unit, transit-area and housing-target laws. What now?
prompt.5: Bill 44 (small-scale multi-unit housing, passed 45 to 29) and Bill 47 (transit-oriented areas, 65 to 0) override municipal zoning; sixteen Metro mayors sought repeal or revision in November 2025. What now?

context.1: The province recently made cities allow more homes on each lot and taller buildings near train stations. City councils used to decide this alone. Many mayors want that power back. Parties disagree on who should decide, and on what the province should do instead.
context.2: In 2023 the province passed laws making cities allow three or four homes on most lots and tall buildings near transit, and set housing targets for cities. Sixteen Metro Vancouver mayors have asked the province to repeal or change those laws. A recent poll found slightly more people back the province than councils. Parties disagree on who should decide.
context.3: The province's 2023 laws require three or four homes on most lots, higher density near transit and housing targets for named cities. Sixteen Metro Vancouver mayors asked in November 2025 to repeal or revise them. The NDP government has kept the laws. CentreBC would keep the transit rules and add provincial approval deadlines. The Conservatives promised in 2024 to scrap the lot rule and pay cities that allow more homes instead, and have no 2026 position. The Greens voted against the lot law.
context.4: Bill 44 (small-scale multi-unit housing) and Bill 47 (transit-oriented areas) passed in November 2023, with housing target orders for named cities. In late November 2025 sixteen Metro Vancouver mayors asked Premier Eby to repeal and revise all three. A Liaison Strategies poll (September 26 to 27, 2026, n=1,000) found 43% would give the province the final say over minimum housing allowances and 37% the council. The NDP has kept the laws. CentreBC keeps transit-area density and adds a provincial approval standard. The Conservatives' 2024 platform pledged to scrap Bill 44 and fund cities that allow multi-unit housing; nothing in 2026. The Greens voted against Bills 44 and 46.
context.5: Bill 44 passed third reading 45 to 29 on November 29, 2023, with Furstenau, Olsen, Rustad and Banman among the nays; Bill 47 passed 65 to 0 on November 30, 2023. Housing Supply Act target orders cover named Metro municipalities. In late November 2025, sixteen mayors (including Burnaby, Richmond, Coquitlam and Delta) wrote to Eby seeking repeal and revision of all three. Liaison Strategies, September 26 to 27, 2026 (n=1,000, plus or minus 3.1): province 43%, council 37% on final say; 56% support more homes nearby. The NDP has no 2026 change; its housing pledges are tax measures. CentreBC's platform sets six-month rezoning and eight-week permit standards with one rulebook by January 1, 2028, a $125 million a year performance fund and a $240 million growth fund. OneBC has no density position.
